before: Inside a giant farmhouse kitchen, the last egg of the season is about to be taken away for breakfast. Two young chicks, Yolkie and Shelly, decide to rescue their unborn sibling and carry it all the way to the safe nest in the garden. The egg is far too big and too fragile for one chick, so they invent the Egg Press: each chick presses one side of the egg with its wing and the two carry it together.
after: Egg Press 3D is a cooperative journey in which two ducks carry a nest containing a fragile egg through a large kitchen and an outdoor obstacle course. Each player controls one duck. Their relative positions determine how the shared nest moves and tilts, so progress depends on communication and careful movement.

before: The journey crosses two worlds. In The Giant Kitchen the chicks must survive slippery butter, a gust from the extractor fan, a launching toaster and a glowing hotplate. In The Garden Hazard they face loose pebbles, swinging branches, a rotating sprinkler and a small stream. A single careless step or a hard knock can crack the shell, so both chicks have to move, jump and brake as one.
after: The first playable map is Kitchen_Map, with preparation counters, stove hazards, a seesaw crossing, cold storage, a pantry and a final patio. It combines traversal with pressure plates, a linked-lights puzzle and a symbol-code lock. The second map, MainMap_Online, uses outdoor platforms, bridges, obstacles, checkpoints and a finish area.

before: Two players connect online. Both play the same kind of character (a chick) with the same abilities; there is no “leader”. The experience is built on communication: one player often has to slow down so the other can catch up, and the player who sees a hazard first has to warn the partner.
after: Two players connect as a host and a client. Both use the same duck player prefab and movement abilities. Each has a player name and an independently selected cosmetic item. The host starts the match and resolves shared gameplay state, but both players participate in carrying the nest.

before: Bright, humorous and slightly dramatic. Cartoon visuals and silly sound effects keep the mood light, while the creaking shell and the growing cracks create real tension. A shared success (reaching the next checkpoint with a healthy egg) is the main emotional reward.
after: The game uses cartoon ducks, colourful scenery and a warm orange interface. Cracks, egg-break visuals, screen feedback and the movement of the nest communicate danger. Reaching a checkpoint gives the pair a shorter recovery route after failure.

before: A 3D physics co-op platformer in which two players carry one fragile egg across dangerous obstacle courses. The egg breaks if the pair moves too fast, accelerates too abruptly, squeezes too hard or suffers a strong impact. The core challenge is synchronisation, not reflexes.
after: A 3D online co-op platformer for two players carrying one nest and egg. Relative movement, height differences, collisions and jump timing can destabilise the egg. Players must navigate the route, solve environmental puzzles and reach the level goal together.

before: Start level → move together and keep the egg stable → jump over / pass hazards → reach a checkpoint (collect score) → reach the goal (or the egg breaks and the pair restarts from the last checkpoint).
after: Menu and equipment selection → create or join a Relay room → host starts with two players → loading and preparation → carry the nest, solve puzzles and collect coins → checkpoint recovery after failure → level victory → next level, replay or return to menu.

before: Physics-driven cooperation: the yolk’s moving centre of mass, shell friction and the spring-damper grip make the egg feel alive and force both players to read the same forces.
after: Shared carrying: the nest is positioned from both players’ carrying points. Distance constraints and the duck rig keep the pair visually connected to it.

before: High stakes, high reward: one mistake can crack the shell, but crossing a narrow board with a perfect partner is very satisfying.
after: Recoverable failure: egg breakage or a player entering a death zone restarts both players and the egg at the current checkpoint, or at the start if no checkpoint has been reached.

before: Readable feedback: every kind of stress (speed, acceleration, squeeze, impact) is visible and audible, so players know why the egg is in danger.
after: Readable feedback: the egg has discrete damage stages, with cracks and local screen feedback. Falling out of the nest is a separate risk from accumulating damage.

before: Distinct visual identity: bright, humorous low-poly style that stays dramatic when the egg cracks.
after: Personal expression: players buy cosmetic head items with coins, preview them in the menu and display their own selected item during online play.

before: The egg loses integrity when the pair moves faster than the safe speed, accelerates too sharply, squeezes too hard or hits something hard. Integrity never regenerates during a run.
after: The egg does not have a 100-point health bar or continuous speed, acceleration or squeeze damage. With progressive damage enabled, eligible damage events increment a counter. Nest collisions can either damage the egg or eject it, as decided by the host.

before: If the egg is destroyed (or the pair falls into a kill zone), both players restart from the last checkpoint with a fresh egg. Each restart costs score.
after: When the egg breaks, both players and the nest restart at the saved checkpoint with a reset egg. Entering a configured Dead zone also restarts the pair. There is no score deduction or limited-life counter in the current round logic.

before: Checkpoints are saved for both players; the run ends successfully when both chicks and the egg enter the goal zone.
after: A checkpoint can be reported by one player; the server validates the contact and safe respawn positions for both. In Kitchen_Map, a player or the nest entering the final trigger can activate victory. In MainMap_Online, NetworkNest checks whether the nest touches Win_Area. The code does not require both ducks and the egg to enter the goal simultaneously.

before: Score = time bonus + integrity bonus + collectible “seeds” − restart penalty. Final stars (1–3) are given from the total score. Scores are shown on the Result screen and compared between the two players’ runs.
after: Coins are the implemented reward currency. A valid online pickup is approved by the server, despawns the shared coin and adds one coin to each connected player’s local wallet. Coins buy cosmetic items in the menu shop. A time score, seed score, restart penalty, star rating and competitive leaderboard are not implemented.

before: Walk at the same speed – decide who leads and call out “slow”, “stop”, “jump” with the ping key or voice chat.
after: Agree on a route and communicate before changing direction or stepping onto a narrow platform. Movement is relative to the local camera.

before: Lean against the direction in which the yolk sways to stabilise it.
after: Keep the players at compatible heights and avoid extreme nest tilt. The egg can roll toward the lower edge and leave the nest when the release angle is exceeded.

before: On butter, release the grip and move in tiny steps; on the toaster, jump together.
after: Use jump timing deliberately. The cooperative jump detector pairs timestamps from different players; a matched pair releases the egg from assisted carrying. In the current maps this can push it sideways out of the nest.

before: Do not stand on the hotplate: the egg slowly boils (heavier, lower jump) – sometimes useful, but not for the high jumps.
after: At puzzle consoles, read the prompt and use E to enter or leave input mode. Solve the lights or symbol code before crossing the opened gate. Esc opens settings; H or F1 toggles the tutorial.

before: Both worlds follow the same design rule, teach – test – twist: a hazard is first introduced in a safe area, then tested with a small risk, then combined with another hazard. Path width shrinks and hazards become more frequent from the beginning to the end of each world, which gives a smooth difficulty curve. Every level has 4–6 checkpoints so a failure never costs more than about one minute.

Route length and completion time depend on player coordination; this report does not assign an unmeasured one-minute maximum loss or fixed completion time.

before: Egg health (integrity) starts at 100 and only decreases. Every physics step the EggStressSystem asks each registered stress source how much damage it produces; impacts are handled in OnCollisionEnter. With e the egg, v its speed, a its acceleration, F the total grip force of both players and J the collision impulse:
after: The server owns the egg simulation and decides damage. Progressive damage is enabled by overrides on the nest instances in both gameplay scenes. Each accepted damage event changes DamageCount; the implementation uses discrete contact events rather than continuous stress formulas.

before: Speed stress: D_speed = k_v · max(0, |v| − v_safe) · Δt
after: First and second damage events: DamageCount increases to 1 and then 2; the visual shows increasing cracks while the phase remains Intact.

before: Acceleration stress: D_acc = k_a · max(0, |a| − a_safe) · Δt  (sudden starts/stops, hard turns)
after: Third damage event: the egg enters Broken and raises the round-failure event. Duplicate contacts on the same object and contacts in the same physics step are filtered.

before: Grip stress: D_grip = k_g · max(0, F − F_safe) · Δt  (over-squeezing or stretching because the players drift apart)
after: Nest impact: after preparation and cooldown checks, the host chooses between applying a damage increment and ejecting the egg. The shared nest prefab currently sets a 0.5 crack probability and a 0.75-second cooldown.

before: Impact: if J ≥ J_break → integrity = 0; else if J ≥ J_crack → D_impact = k_i · (J − J_crack)
after: Release and landing: ReleaseCarry marks the egg to break at its next eligible environment collision, even if it has fewer than two prior damage increments. Nest and player colliders, triggers and Win_Area are excluded from ordinary environment damage checks.

before: Multiplier: while the egg is Cracked all damage is multiplied by 1.5.
after: Recovery: NetworkRoundManager responds to egg failure with a checkpoint restart. The egg lifecycle also breaks an actively simulated egg below world Y = −50 as a safety fallback.

before: For a raw egg a lightweight spring-damper simulates the yolk: the yolk offset follows the opposite of the egg’s local acceleration, is pulled back to the centre by a spring and damped by friction. The offset is then written to Rigidbody.centerOfMass (scaled by a small influence factor). The result is a wobble that grows when players accelerate abruptly and that can be damped with the Q/E lean – the physics-driven balance pillar without simulating a second rigid body.
after: NestEggCarryPhysics simulates a bounded egg offset on the nest floor using gravity, a small inertial contribution and damping. While carried, the body is moved in the nest coordinate system. Excessive tilt or paired jump events release it to server-side Rigidbody motion. There is no simulated internal yolk, raw-to-boiled conversion, player-controlled squeeze or Q/E balancing mechanic.

before: EggStateMachine contains five states. Idle and Rolling describe the motion on the ground, Jumping describes airtime, Cracked is entered once integrity falls below 60 and Destroyed is the terminal state. In CrackedState the motion checks still run (the egg can still roll or jump), but the stability and damage multipliers change.
after: NestEggPhase defines Waiting, Intact and Broken. Waiting covers setup; reset activates Intact; breaking activates Broken; a round restart creates the next intact simulation state. DamageCount 1 and 2 do not create separate Cracked or Critical states. Player movement separately uses an Idle/Walk state machine, with jump handled by the motor.

Waiting → preparation/reset → Intact → break condition → Broken
Broken → checkpoint restart/reset → Intact
Any active phase → stop/wait for preparation → Waiting

DamageCount within Intact: 0 → 1 → 2.
The next accepted damage event, or an eligible landing after release, produces Broken.
Figure 8: Egg lifecycle and separate damage counter

before: The egg is held by two custom spring-damper forces instead of Unity joints. This is more tunable, it exposes the exact force magnitude to the stress system and it is easier to replicate: the only authority needed is the host’s physics step.
after: The pair carries the nest through carrying anchors, geometry calculations and distance constraints. The player motor uses CharacterController. The nest follows the shared carry pose, while the egg uses assisted carrying or free Rigidbody motion. The current system does not apply two player-controlled spring grips directly to the eggshell.

before: This section explains how SOLID principles and design patterns are applied in the project. For each item, insert a screenshot of the relevant code and write 2–3 sentences below it explaining what the code does and why the principle or pattern was used.
after: The following examples refer to implemented classes. Interfaces separate input, movement constraints, wallet access, Relay service calls and puzzle interactions. The project also retains direct references and singleton services, so these examples describe specific applications of SOLID rather than claiming that every class follows every principle.

S — Single Responsibility: KeyboardPlayerInput reads movement/jump input; PlayerCharacterMotor applies movement; PlayerAnimationPresenter controls animation. These responsibilities are separated from session setup and UI.
O — Open/Closed: PlayerCharacterMotor accepts IPlayerMovementConstraint. The motor can use a different constraint implementation without changing its movement calculation.
L — Liskov Substitution: OnlineIdleState and OnlineWalkState implement OnlinePlayerState. OnlinePlayerStateMachine calls the same Enter, Tick and Exit contract regardless of the active state.

I — Interface Segregation: ICoinWallet exposes the wallet operations needed by coin collection; IPlayerMovementConstraint exposes movement limiting; IPuzzleInteractable exposes puzzle activation. Consumers do not depend on a large all-purpose game manager.
Example: Coin receives an ICoinWallet through Initialize; it calls AddCoin after collection. Puzzle controllers reference IPuzzleInteractable to activate their gate.

D — Dependency Inversion: RelaySession receives IRelayRoomService in its constructor, and coin collection receives ICoinWallet. Unity-facing installers connect concrete implementations to those contracts.

State pattern: OnlinePlayerStateMachine changes between OnlineIdleState and OnlineWalkState. Jump input is passed separately to the motor; the egg uses an enum lifecycle rather than the five-state class hierarchy proposed in the original report.

before: NOTE FOR TEAM – Insert code screenshot: EggStateMachine (ChangeState) + one concrete state (e.g. RollingState) and, if you want, GameManager states (Menu, Lobby, Playing, Result). Optionally add the egg state diagram (Figure “Egg state machine”) next to it.
after: The state-machine example is Assets/Scripts/Player/Movement/OnlinePlayerStateMachine.cs. ChangeState calls Exit on the previous state and Enter on the next state, while Tick delegates movement decisions to the current state.

Strategy-style composition: IPlayerMovementConstraint lets PlayerCharacterMotor delegate movement limits. CarryDistanceConstraint supplies the current carrying constraint. This separates movement integration from the rule that keeps two carriers within reach.

Observer pattern: CurrencyManager raises OnCoinChanged after AddCoin or a successful SpendCoin. CoinUI subscribes, updates its TextMeshPro label and unsubscribes when destroyed. RoomLobbyView similarly listens to roster changes; equipment visuals listen to the equipped-ID NetworkVariable.

Singleton usage: SaveSystem, CurrencyManager, PlayerInventory and CharacterEquipment provide shared access in the existing implementation. They simplify access but require correct scene lifetime and initialisation. No Object Pool or HazardBase Template Method is claimed for the current gameplay.

Network synchronisation: player movement is owner-authoritative; shared nest/egg state, checkpoint decisions and round outcomes are server-controlled. NetworkVariables carry persistent state and RPCs carry requests/events. Nest snapshots include both nest and egg data, and the client uses prediction, reconciliation and presentation smoothing.

The screenshots and numerical results retained below belong to the earlier report. They document a historical capture, not a benchmark of the current scripts and levels. A new comparison must use the same hardware, resolution, quality settings, build type and capture duration for host and client.

before: Observation: The Profiler recorded a massive number of Batches (4725) with the Saved by batching metric at 0. For a standard 3D game, especially on mobile platforms, this number should ideally be maintained under 500–1000 batches.
after: The earlier report records 4,725 batches for a gameplay capture. This is a useful optimisation lead, but the count depends on the scene, camera and render passes. It is not a universal limit or a current-build measurement.

before: Technical Cause: In Unity's rendering pipeline, each Batch typically represents a Draw Call—a set of instructions the CPU must prepare and send to the GPU to render an object. With nearly 5000 individual draw calls, the CPU spends an excessive amount of time packaging data (material states, shaders, meshes) to send across the system bus. The fact that batching is saving zero draw calls indicates that the engine is rendering every single object entirely independently without grouping them.
after: A high batch count can increase render-thread submission cost. A zero “Saved by batching” statistic alone does not prove that every batching path is disabled; SRP Batcher behaviour must be inspected separately in the Frame Debugger.

before: Enable Static Batching: Mark all static environmental objects (buildings, roads, terrain) with the Static flag in the Inspector. Unity will automatically combine their meshes, drastically reducing the number of draw calls.
after: Evaluate static batching for suitable non-moving environment meshes, checking the memory cost and the render-pipeline configuration.

before: Utilize GPU Instancing: Apply this technique for objects that share the same Mesh and Material but appear in large quantities (e.g., coins, trees, repeating obstacles). This allows the GPU to render thousands of identical objects using only a single draw call.
after: Evaluate GPU instancing for repeated compatible mesh/material combinations, and compare frame time before and after. Do not assume every repeated object can be reduced to a single draw call.

before: Observation: The game is forcing the GPU to render 9.4 million Triangles and 9.8 million Vertices per frame. This is an extraordinarily heavy workload, typically only seen in high-end AAA PC or Console titles.
after: The earlier capture reports approximately 9.4 million triangles and 9.8 million vertices. These are recorded rendering statistics and should be remeasured with the current content and camera views.

before: Technical Cause: Processing nearly 10 million polygons per frame overloads both the vertex and pixel shaders. The GPU consumes massive memory bandwidth and computing power (FLOPS) just to calculate spatial positions and colors for geometric details that likely do not contribute significantly to the visual experience. This sheer volume of geometry is the primary driver of the GPU Bound state (FPS dropping to 23.7).
after: High visible geometry can add GPU work. To establish the bottleneck, compare GPU timing and controlled changes to resolution, shadows and geometry. The FPS value and polygon count alone do not prove a GPU-bound frame.

before: Asset Optimization (Low-Poly): Review and replace the current 3D models with decimated, low-poly versions. Rely on Textures and Normal Maps to fake surface details instead of using dense geometry.
after: Review dense models and reduce detail that is not visible at gameplay distance. Preserve the silhouette and important visual features.

before: Implement Level of Detail (LOD): Configure LOD Groups so that Unity automatically swaps to lower-polygon models when objects are further away from the camera, only rendering high-poly meshes when the player is close.
after: Evaluate LOD Groups for distant environment assets and verify transitions during actual camera movement.

before: Apply Occlusion Culling: Set up Occlusion Culling so the engine completely stops rendering objects that are hidden behind larger foreground elements, immediately reducing the number of rendered polygons.
after: Evaluate occlusion culling where level geometry can hide substantial content; measure its benefit against the cost and bake requirements.

before: Observation: There are currently 2333 objects simultaneously casting shadows within the scene.
after: The earlier report records 2,333 shadow casters in the captured view. The number is historical and varies with scene visibility and shadow settings.

before: Technical Cause: To generate real-time shadows, Unity uses a technique called Shadow Mapping. This requires the engine to render the scene multiple times from the perspective of the light source (Directional Light) into a depth map before determining which pixels are in shadow. Calculating this for over 2300 objects drains a massive amount of the GPU's fillrate and system bandwidth, severely impacting frame rates.
after: Shadow passes render additional geometry from the light’s view. Shadow distance, cascades and the number of visible casters should be measured alongside GPU timing before selecting a change.

before: Disable Shadows for Minor Objects: Select all minor, decorative, or distant objects (such as grass, small rocks, or background props) and disable the Cast Shadows option in their Mesh Renderer components.
after: Disable shadow casting on minor or distant decorative objects where it does not affect readability.

before: Bake Lighting: Transition the static environment to pre-calculated Lightmaps. Change the Directional Light mode to Mixed so that expensive real-time shadows are only calculated for dynamic, moving objects (like the player and enemies), while the environment uses baked shadows.
after: Evaluate baked or mixed lighting for static scenery while retaining suitable dynamic shadows for ducks, the nest and moving objects. Compare quality and performance rather than assuming this conversion is already complete.
